entries.4c54ab0ef13805ec3a19f9e6000ec564b810d9af: <div sID="gen17518" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Jer.15" sID="Jer.15"/> <div eID="gen17518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17519" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17520" type="x-p"/> When we left the prophet, in the close of the foregoing chapter, so pathetically poring out his prayers before God, we had reason to hope that in this chapter we should find God reconciled to the land and the prophet brought into a quiet composed frame; but, to our great surprise, we find it much otherwise as to both. I. Notwithstanding the prophet's prayers, God here ratifies the sentence given against the people, and abandons them to ruin turning a deaf ear to all the intercessions made for them, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1-Jer.15.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. The prophet himself, notwithstanding the satisfaction he had in communion with God, still finds himself uneasy and out of temper. 1. He complains to God of his continual struggle with his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">ver. 10</reference>. 2. God assures him that he shall be taken under special protection, though there was a general desolation coming upon the land, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.11-Jer.15.14">ver. 11-14</reference>. 3. He appeals to God concerning his sincerity in the discharge of his prophetic office and thinks it hard that he should not have more of the comfort of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.15-Jer.15.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. 4. Fresh security is given him that, upon condition he continue faithful, God will continue his care of him and his favour to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.19-Jer.15.21">ver. 19-21</reference>. And thus, at length, we hope he regained the possession of his own soul.
entries.79df3f0ee185d5989b25001fd54823e4d594d70c: <div eID="gen17520" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17519" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sentence against Judah Confirmed; Destruction of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17521" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then said the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> my mind <hi type="italic">could</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> toward this people: cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> out of my sight, and let them go forth. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it shall come to pass, if they say unto thee, Whither shall we go forth? then thou shalt tell them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Such as <hi type="italic">are</hi> for death, to death; and such as <hi type="italic">are</hi> for the sword, to the sword; and such as <hi type="italic">are</hi> for the famine, to the famine; and such as <hi type="italic">are</hi> for the captivity, to the captivity. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy. <hi type="super">4</hi> And I will cause them to be removed into all kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah king of Judah, for <hi type="italic">that</hi> which he did in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">5</hi> For who shall have pity upon thee, O Jerusalem? or who shall bemoan thee? or who shall go aside to ask how thou doest? <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou hast forsaken me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thou art gone backward: therefore will I stretch out my hand against thee, and destroy thee; I am weary with repenting. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave <hi type="italic">them</hi> of children, I will destroy my people, <hi type="italic">since</hi> they return not from their ways. <hi type="super">8</hi> Their widows are increased to me above the sand of the seas: I have brought upon them against the mother of the young men a spoiler at noonday: I have caused <hi type="italic">him</hi> to fall upon it suddenly, and terrors upon the city. <hi type="super">9</hi> She that hath borne seven languisheth: she hath given up the ghost; her sun is gone down while <hi type="italic">it was</hi> yet day: she hath been ashamed and confounded: and the residue of them will I deliver to the sword before their enemies, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17522" type="x-p"/> We scarcely find any where more pathetic expressions of divine wrath against a provoking people than we have here in these verses. The prophet had prayed earnestly for them, and found some among them to join with him; and yet not so much as a reprieve was gained, nor the least mitigation of the judgment; but this answer is given to the prophet's prayers, that the decree had gone forth, was irreversible, and would shortly be executed. Observe here, <div eID="gen17522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17523" type="x-p"/> I. What the sin was upon which this severe sentence was grounded. 1. It is in remembrance of a former iniquity; it is because of Manasseh, for that which he did in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.4">v. 4</reference>. What that was we are told, and that it was for it that Jerusalem was destroyed, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.3-2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 3, 4</reference>. It was for his idolatry, and <hi type="italic">the innocent blood which he shed, which the Lord would not pardon.</hi> He is called <hi type="italic">the son of Hezekiah</hi> because his relation to so good a father was a great aggravation of his sin, so far was it from being an excuse of it. The greatest part of a generation was worn off since Manasseh's time, yet his sin is brought into the account; as in Jerusalem's last ruin God brought upon it all <hi type="italic">the righteous blood shed on the earth,</hi> to show how heavy the guilt of blood will light and lie somewhere, sooner or later, and that reprieves are not pardons. 2. It is in consideration of their present impenitence. See how their sin is described (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast forsaken me,</hi> my service and thy duty to me; <hi type="italic">thou hast gone backward</hi> into the ways of contradiction, art become the reverse of what thou shouldst have been and of what God by his law would have led thee forward to." See how the impenitence is described (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They return not from their ways,</hi> the ways of their own hearts, into the ways of God's commandments again. There is mercy for those who have turned aside if they will return; but what favour can those expect that persist in their apostasy? <div eID="gen17523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17524" type="x-p"/> II. What the sentence is. It is such as denotes no less than an utter ruin. <div eID="gen17524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17525" type="x-p"/> 1. God himself abandons and abhors them: <hi type="italic">My mind cannot be towards them.</hi> How can it be thought that the holy God should have any remaining complacency in those that have such a rooted antipathy to him? It is not in a passion, but with a just and holy indignation, that he says, "<hi type="italic">Cast them out of my sight,</hi> as that which is in the highest degree odious and offensive, and <hi type="italic">let them go forth,</hi> for I will be troubled with them no more." <div eID="gen17525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17526" type="x-p"/> 2. He will not admit any intercession to be made for them (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Though Moses and Samuel stood before me,</hi> by prayer or sacrifice to reconcile me to them, yet I could not be prevailed with to admit them into favour." Moses and Samuel were two as great favourites of Heaven as ever were the blessings of this earth, and were particularly famed for the success of their mediation between God and his offending people; many a time they would have been destroyed if Moses had not stood before him in the breach; and to Samuel's prayers they owed their lives (<reference osisRef="1Sam.12.19">1 Sam. xii. 19</reference>); yet even their intercessions should not prevail, no, not though they were now in a state of perfection, much less Jeremiah's who was now <hi type="italic">a man subject to like passions</hi> as others. The putting of this as a case, <hi type="italic">Though they should stand before me,</hi> supposes that they do not, and is an intimation that saints in heaven are not intercessors for saints on earth. It is the prerogative of the Eternal Word to be the only Mediator in <hi type="italic">the other world,</hi> whatever Moses, and Samuel, and others were in this. <div eID="gen17526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17527" type="x-p"/> 3. He condemns them all to one destroying judgment or other. When God casts them out of his presence, <hi type="italic">whither shall they go forth?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">v. 2</reference>. Certainly nowhere to be safe or easy, but to be met by one judgment while they are pursued by another, till they find themselves surrounded with mischiefs on all hands, so that they cannot escape; <hi type="italic">Such as are for death to death.</hi> By death here is meant the pestilence (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.8">Rev. vi. 8</reference>), for it is death without visible means. <hi type="italic">Such as are for death to death,</hi> or <hi type="italic">for the sword to the sword;</hi> every man shall perish in that way that God has appointed: the law that appoints the malefactor's death determines what death he shall die. Or, He that is by his own choice for this judgment, let him take it, or for that, let him take it, but by the one or the other they shall all fall and none shall escape. It is a choice like that which David was put to, and was thereby put into a <hi type="italic">great strait,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.14">2 Sam. xxiv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Captivity</hi> is mentioned last, some think, because the sorest judgment of all, it being both a complication and continuance of miseries. That of <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> is again repeated (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.3">v. 3</reference>), and is made the first of another four frightful set of destroyers, which God will <hi type="italic">appoint over them,</hi> as officers over the soldiers, to do what they please with them. As those that escape <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> shall be cut off by pestilence, famine, or captivity, so those that fall by the sword shall be cut off by divine vengeance, which pursues sinners on the other side death; there shall be <hi type="italic">dogs to tear</hi> in the field to devour. And, if there be any that think to outrun justice, they shall be made the most public monuments of it: <hi type="italic">They shall be removed into all kingdoms of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.4">v. 4</reference>), like Cain, who, that he might be made a spectacle of horror to all, became <hi type="italic">a fugitive and a vagabond</hi> in the earth. <div eID="gen17527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17528" type="x-p"/> 4. They shall fall without being relieved. Who can do any thing to help them? for (1.) God, even their own God (so he had been) appears against them: <hi type="italic">I will stretch out my hand against thee,</hi> which denotes a deliberate determined stroke, which will reach far and wound deeply. <hi type="italic">I am weary with repenting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.6">v. 6</reference>); it is a strange expression; they had behaved so provokingly, especially by their treacherous professions of repentance, that they had put even infinite patience itself to the stretch. God had often turned away his wrath when it was ready to break forth against them; but now he will grant no more reprieves. Miserable is the case of those who have sinned so long against God's mercy that at length they have sinned it away. (2.) Their own country expels them, and is ready to <hi type="italic">spue them out,</hi> as it had done the Canaanites that were before them; for so it was threatened (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">Lev. xviii. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land,</hi> in their own gates, through which they shall be scattered, or <hi type="italic">into the gates of the earth,</hi> into the cities of all the nations about them, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">v. 7</reference>. (3.) Their own children, that should assist them when they speak with the enemy in the gate, shall be cut off from them: <hi type="italic">I will bereave them of children,</hi> so that they shall have little hopes that the next generation will retrieve their affairs, for <hi type="italic">I will destroy my people;</hi> and, when the inhabitants are slain, the land will soon be desolate. This melancholy article is enlarged upon, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8-Jer.15.9">v. 8, 9</reference>, where we have, [1.] The destroyer brought upon them. When God has bloody work to do he will find out bloody instruments to do it with. Nebuchadnezzar is here called <hi type="italic">a spoiler at noon-day,</hi> not a thief in the night, that is afraid of being discovered, but one that without fear shall break through and destroy all the fences of rights and properties, and this in the face of the sun and in defiance of its light: <hi type="italic">I have brought against the mother a young man, a spoiler</hi> (so some read it); for Nebuchadnezzar, when he first invaded Judah, was but a <hi type="italic">young man,</hi> in the first year of his reign. We read it, <hi type="italic">I have brought upon them,</hi> even <hi type="italic">against the mother of the young men, a spoiler,</hi> that is, against Jerusalem, a mother city, that had a very numerous family of young men: or that invasion was in a particular manner terrible to those mothers who had many sons fit for war, who must now hazard their lives in the high places of the field, and, being an unequal match for the enemy, would be likely to fall there, to the inexpressible grief of their poor mothers, who had nursed them up with a great deal of tenderness. The same God that brought the spoiler upon them <hi type="italic">caused him to fall upon it,</hi> that is, upon the spoil delivered to him, <hi type="italic">suddenly</hi> and by surprise; and then <hi type="italic">terrors</hi> came <hi type="italic">upon the city.</hi> the original is very abrupt—<hi type="italic">the city and terrors. O the city!</hi> what a consternation will it then be in! <hi type="italic">O the terrors</hi> that shall then seize it! Then the city and terrors shall be brought together, that seemed at a distance from each other. <hi type="italic">I will cause to fall suddenly upon her</hi> (upon Jerusalem) <hi type="italic">a watcher and terrors;</hi> so Mr. Gataker reads it, for the word is used for a watcher (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.13">Dan. iv. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.23">23</reference>), and the Chaldean soldiers were called watchers, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.16">ch. iv. 16</reference>. [2.] The destruction made by this destroyer. A dreadful slaughter is here described. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The wives are deprived of their husbands: <hi type="italic">Their widows are increased above the sand of the seas,</hi> so numerous have they now grown. It was promised that the men of Israel (for those only were numbered) should be <hi type="italic">as the sand of the sea for multitude;</hi> but now <hi type="italic">they</hi> shall be all cut off, and their widows shall be so. But observe, God says, <hi type="italic">They are increased to me.</hi> Though the husbands were cut off by the sword of his justice, their poor widows were gathered in the arms of his mercy, who has taken it among the titles of his honour to be <hi type="italic">the God of the widows.</hi> Widows are said to be <hi type="italic">taken into the number,</hi> the number of those whom God has a particular compassion and concern for. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The parents are deprived of their children: <hi type="italic">She that has borne seven</hi> sons, whom she expected to be the support and joy of her age, now <hi type="italic">languishes,</hi> when she has seen them all cut off by the sword in one day, who had been many years her burden and care. <hi type="italic">She that had many children has waxed feeble,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1 Sam. ii. 5</reference>. See what uncertain comforts children are; and let us therefore rejoice in them <hi type="italic">as though we rejoiced not.</hi> When the children are slain the mother <hi type="italic">gives up the ghost,</hi> for her life was bound up in theirs: <hi type="italic">Her sun has gone down while it was yet day;</hi> she is bereaved of all her comforts just when she thought herself in the midst of the enjoyment of them. She is now <hi type="italic">ashamed and confounded</hi> to think how proud she was of her sons, how fond of them, and how much she promised herself from them. Some understand, by this languishing mother, Jerusalem lamenting the death of her inhabitants as passionately as ever poor mother bewailed her children. Many are cut off already, <hi type="italic">and the residue of them,</hi> who have yet escaped, and, as was hoped, were reserved to be the seed of another generation, even these <hi type="italic">will I deliver to the sword before their enemies</hi> (as the condemned malefactor is delivered to the sheriff to be executed), <hi type="italic">saith the Lord,</hi> the Judge of heaven and earth, who, we are sure, herein judges according to truth, though the judgment seem severe. <div eID="gen17528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17529" type="x-p"/> 5. They shall fall without being pitied (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For who shall have pity on thee, O Jerusalem?</hi> When thy God has <hi type="italic">cast thee out of his sight,</hi> and his compassions fail and are shut up from thee, neither thy enemies nor thy friends shall have any compassion for thee. They shall have no sympathy with thee; they shall not <hi type="italic">bemoan thee</hi> nor be sorry for thee; they shall have no concern for thee, shall not go a step out of their way to <hi type="italic">ask how thou dost.</hi>" For, (1.) Their friends, who were expected to do these friendly offices, were all involved with them in the calamities, and had enough to do to bemoan themselves. (2.) It was plain to all their neighbours that they had brought all this misery upon themselves by their obstinacy in sin, and that they might easily have prevented it by repentance and reformation, which they were often in vain called to; and therefore <hi type="italic">who can pity them? O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself.</hi> Those will perish for ever unpitied that might have been saved upon such easy terms and would not. (3.) God will thus complete their misery. He will set their acquaintance, as he did Job's at a distance from them; and his hand, his righteous hand, is to be acknowledged in all the unkindnesses of our friends, as well as in all the injuries done us by our foes.
entries.fdcb7b5adb017e111af71a3d3866a139b047bbe3: <div eID="gen17529" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Complaint; The Prophet Assured of His Safety. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17530" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have neither lent on usury, nor men have lent to me on usury; <hi type="italic">yet</hi> every one of them doth curse me. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Verily it shall be well with thy remnant; verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee <hi type="italic">well</hi> in the time of evil and in the time of affliction. <hi type="super">12</hi> Shall iron break the northern iron and the steel? <hi type="super">13</hi> Thy substance and thy treasures will I give to the spoil without price, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> for all thy sins, even in all thy borders. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will make <hi type="italic">thee</hi> to pass with thine enemies into a land <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou knowest not: for a fire is kindled in mine anger, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall burn upon you. <div eID="gen17530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17531" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah has now returned from his public work and retired into his closet; what passed between him and his God there we have an account of in these and the following verses, which he published afterwards, to affect the people with the weight and importance of his messages to them. Here is, <div eID="gen17531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17532" type="x-p"/> I. The complaint which the prophet makes to God of the many discouragements he met with in his work, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">v. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen17532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17533" type="x-p"/> 1. He met with a great deal of contradiction and opposition. He was a <hi type="italic">man of strife and contention to the whole land</hi> (so it might be read, rather than to <hi type="italic">the whole earth,</hi> for his business lay only in that land); both city and country quarrelled with him, and set themselves against him, and said and did all they could to thwart him. He was a peaceable man, gave no provocation to any, nor was apt to resent the provocations given him, and yet <hi type="italic">a man of strife,</hi> not a man striving, but a man striven with; he was for peace, but, when he spoke, they were for war. And, whatever they pretended, that which was the real cause of their quarrels with him was his faithfulness to God and to their souls. He showed them their sins that were working their ruin, and put them into a way to prevent that ruin, which was the greatest kindness he could do them; and yet this was it for which they were incensed against him and looked upon him as their enemy. Even the prince of peace himself was thus a man of strife, a sign spoken against, continually <hi type="italic">enduring the contradiction of sinners against himself.</hi> And the gospel of peace brings division, even to fire and sword, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.34-Matt.10.35 ">Matt. x. 34, 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.49-Luke.12.51">Luke xii. 49, 51</reference>. Now this made Jeremiah very uneasy, even to a degree of impatience. He cried out, <hi type="italic">Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me,</hi> as if it were his mother's fault that she bore him, and he had better never have been born than be born to such an uncomfortable life; nay, he is angry that she had <hi type="italic">borne him a man of strife,</hi> as if he had been fatally determined to this by the stars that were in the ascendant at his birth. If he had any meaning of this kind, doubtless it was very much his infirmity; we rather hope it was intended for no more than a pathetic lamentation of his own case. Note, (1.) Even those who are most quiet and peaceable, if they serve God faithfully, are often made men of strife. We can but <hi type="italic">follow peace;</hi> we have the making only of one side of the bargain, and therefore can but, <hi type="italic">as much as in us lies, live peaceably.</hi> (2.) It is very uncomfortable to those who are of a peaceable disposition to live among those who are continually picking quarrels with them. (3.) Yet, if we cannot live so peaceably as we desire with our neighbours, we must not be so disturbed at it as thereby to lose the repose of our own minds and put ourselves upon the fret. <div eID="gen17533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17534" type="x-p"/> 2. He met with a great deal of contempt, contumely, and reproach. They every one of them cursed him; they branded him as a turbulent factious man, as an incendiary and a sower of discord and sedition. They ought to have blessed him, and to have blessed God for him; but they had arrived at such a pitch of enmity against God and his word that for his sake they cursed his messenger, spoke ill of him, wished ill to him, did all they could to make him odious. They all did so; he had scarcely one friend in Judah or Jerusalem that would give him a good word. Note, It is often the lot of the best of men to have the worst of characters ascribed to them. <hi type="italic">So persecuted they the prophets.</hi> But one would be apt to suspect that surely Jeremiah had given them some provocation, else he could not have lost himself thus: no, not the least: <hi type="italic">I have neither lent</hi> money <hi type="italic">nor borrowed</hi> money, have been neither creditor nor debtor; for so general is the signification of the words here. (1.) It is implied here that those who deal much in the business of this world are often involved thereby in strife and contention; <hi type="italic">meum et tuum—mine and thine</hi> are the great make-bates; lenders and borrowers sue and are sued, and great dealers often get a great deal of ill-will. (2.) it was an instance of Jeremiah's great prudence, and it is written for our learning, that, being called to be a prophet, he <hi type="italic">entangled not himself in the affairs of this life,</hi> but kept clear from them, that he might apply the more closely to the business of his profession and might not give the least shadow of suspicion that he aimed at secular advantages in it nor any occasion to his neighbours to contend with him. He <hi type="italic">put out</hi> no money, for he was no usurer, nor indeed had he any money to lend: he <hi type="italic">took up</hi> no money, for he was no purchaser, no merchant, no spendthrift. He was perfectly dead to this world and the things of it: a very little served to keep him, and we find (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.2">ch. xvi. 2</reference>) that he had neither wife nor children to keep. And yet, (3.) Though he behaved thus discreetly, and so as one would think should have gained him universal esteem, yet he lay under a general odium, through the iniquity of the times. Blessed be God, bad as things are with us, they are not so bad but that there are those with whom virtue has its praise; yet let not those who behave most prudently think it strange if they have not the respect and esteem they deserve. <hi type="italic">Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you.</hi> <div eID="gen17534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17535" type="x-p"/> II. The answer which God gave to this complaint. Though there was in it a mixture of passion and infirmity, yet God graciously took cognizance of it, because it was <hi type="italic">for his sake</hi> that the prophet suffered reproach. In this answer, 1. God assures him that he should weather the storm and be made easy at last, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.11">v. 11</reference>. Though his neighbours quarrelled with him for what he did in the discharge of his office, yet God accepted him and promised to stand by him. It is in the original expressed in the form of an oath: "<hi type="italic">If I</hi> take not care of thee, let me never be counted faithful; <hi type="italic">verily it shall go well with thy remnant,</hi> with the remainder of thy life" (for so the word signifies); "the residue of thy days shall be more comfortable to thee than those hitherto have been." <hi type="italic">Thy end shall be good;</hi> so the Chaldee reads it. Note, It is a great and sufficient support to the people of God that, how troublesome soever their way may be, it shall be well with them in their latter end, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Ps. xxxvii. 37</reference>. They have still a <hi type="italic">remnant,</hi> a <hi type="italic">residue,</hi> something behind and left in reserve, which will be sufficient to counterbalance all their grievances, and the hope of it may serve to make them easy. It should seem that Jeremiah, besides the vexation that his people gave him, was uneasy at the apprehension he had of sharing largely in the public judgments which he foresaw coming; and, though he mentioned not this, God replied to his thought of it, as to Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.19">Exod. iv. 19</reference>. Jeremiah thought, "If my friends are thus abusive to me, what will my enemies be?" And God had thought fit to awaken in him an expectation of this kind, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">ch. xii. 5</reference>. But here he quiets his mind with this promise: "<hi type="italic">Verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil,</hi> when all about thee shall be laid waste." Note, God has all men's hearts in his hand, and can turn those to favour his servants whom they were most afraid of. And the prophets of the Lord have often met with fairer and better treatment among open enemies than among those that call themselves his people. When we see trouble coming, and it looks very threatening, let us not despair, but hope in God, because it may prove better than we expect. This promise was accomplished when Nebuchadnezzar, having taken the city, charged the captain of the guard to be kind to Jeremiah, and let him have every thing he had a mind to, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.11-Jer.39.12">ch. xxxix. 11, 12</reference>. The following words, <hi type="italic">Shall iron break the northern iron, and the steel,</hi> or <hi type="italic">brass?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.12">v. 12</reference>), being compared with the promise of God made to Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>), that he would make him an <hi type="italic">iron pillar</hi> and <hi type="italic">brazen walls,</hi> seem intended for his comfort. They were continually clashing with him, and were rough and hard as iron; but Jeremiah, being armed with power and courage from on high, is as northern iron, which is naturally stronger, and as steel, which is hardened by art; and therefore they shall not prevail against him; compare this with <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.6">Ezek. ii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.8-Ezek.3.9">iii. 8, 9</reference>. He might the better bear their quarrelling with him when he was sure of the victory. 2. God assures him that his enemies and persecutors should be lost in the storm, should be ruined at last, and that therein the word of God in his mouth should be accomplished and he proved a true prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.13-Jer.15.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. God here turns his speech from the prophet to the people. To them also <reference osisRef="Jer.15.12">v. 12</reference> may be applied: <hi type="italic">Shall iron break the northern iron, and the steel?</hi> Shall their courage and strength, and the most hardly and vigorous of their efforts, be able to contest either with the counsel of God or with the army of the Chaldeans, which are as inflexible, as invincible, as the northern iron and steel. Let them therefore hear their doom: <hi type="italic">Thy substance and thy treasure will I give to the spoil,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">without price;</hi> the spoilers shall have it <hi type="italic">gratis;</hi> it shall be to them a cheap and easy prey. Observe, The prophet was poor; he neither lent nor borrowed; he had nothing to lose, neither <hi type="italic">substance</hi> nor <hi type="italic">treasure,</hi> and therefore the enemy will treat him well, <hi type="italic">Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator—The traveller that has no property about him will congratulate himself when accosted by a robber.</hi> But the people that had great estates in money and land would be slain for what they had, or the enemy, finding they had much, would use them hardly, to make them confess more. And it is their own iniquity that herein corrects them: It is <hi type="italic">for all thy sins, even in all thy borders.</hi> All parts of the country, even those which lay most remote, had contributed to the national guilt, and all shall now be brought to account. Let not one tribe lay the blame upon another, but each take shame to itself: It is for <hi type="italic">all thy sins in all thy borders.</hi> Thus shall they stay at home till they see their estates ruined, and then they shall be carried into captivity, to spend the sad remains of a miserable life in slavery: "<hi type="italic">I will make thee to pass with thy enemies,</hi> who shall lead thee in triumph <hi type="italic">into a land that thou knowest not,</hi> and therefore canst expect to find no comfort in it." All this is the fruit of God's wrath: "It is <hi type="italic">a fire kindled in my anger, which shall burn upon you,</hi> and, if not extinguished in time, will burn eternally."
entries.7d9cb326d4e24cdc35ed62b64bc5248d920716b5: <div eID="gen17535" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Humble Appeal to God; God's Answer to Jeremiah's Address. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  606.)</title> <div sID="gen17536" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou knowest: remember me, and visit me, and revenge me of my persecutors; take me not away in thy longsuffering: know that for thy sake I have suffered rebuke. <hi type="super">16</hi> Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart: for I am called by thy name, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of hosts. <hi type="super">17</hi> I sat not in the assembly of the mockers, nor rejoiced; I sat alone because of thy hand: for thou hast filled me with indignation. <hi type="super">18</hi> Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, <hi type="italic">which</hi> refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, <hi type="italic">and as</hi> waters <hi type="italic">that</hi> fail? <hi type="super">19</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , If thou return, then will I bring thee again, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou shalt stand before me: and if thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth: let them return unto thee; but return not thou unto them. <hi type="super">20</hi> And I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with thee to save thee and to deliver thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">21</hi> And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem thee out of the hand of the terrible. <div eID="gen17536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17537" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, we have, <div eID="gen17537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17538" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet's humble address to God, containing a representation both of his integrity and of the hardships he underwent notwithstanding. It is a matter of comfort to us that, whatever ails us, we have a God to go to, before whom we may spread our case and to whose omniscience we may appeal, as the prophet here, "<hi type="italic">O Lord! thou knowest;</hi> thou knowest my sincerity, which men are resolved they will not acknowledge; thou knowest my distress, which men disdain to take notice of." Observe here, <div eID="gen17538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17539" type="x-p"/> 1. What it is that the prophet prays for, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) That God would consider his case and be mindful of him: "<hi type="italic">O Lord! remember me;</hi> think upon me for good." (2.) That God would communicate strength and comfort to him: "<hi type="italic">Visit me;</hi> not only remember me, but let me know that thou rememberest me, that thou art nigh unto me." (3.) That he would appear for him against those that did him wrong: <hi type="italic">Revenge me of my persecutors,</hi> or rather, <hi type="italic">Vindicate me from my persecutors;</hi> give judgment against them, and let that judgment be executed so far as is necessary for my vindication and to compel them to acknowledge that they have done me wrong. Further than this a good man will not desire that God should avenge him. Let something be done to convince the world that (whatever blasphemers say to the contrary) Jeremiah is a righteous man and the God whom he serves is a righteous God. (4.) That he would yet spare him and continue him in the land of the living: "<hi type="italic">Take me not away</hi> by a sudden stroke, but <hi type="italic">in thy long-suffering</hi> lengthen out my days." The best men will own themselves so obnoxious to God's wrath that they are indebted to his patience for the continuance of their lives. Or, "While thou exercisest long-suffering towards my persecutors, let not them prevail to take me away." Though in a passion he complained of his birth (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">v. 10</reference>), yet he desires here that his death might not be hastened; for life is sweet to nature, and the life of a useful man is so to grace. <hi type="italic">I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world.</hi> <div eID="gen17539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17540" type="x-p"/> 2. What it is that he pleads with God for mercy and relief against his enemies, persecutors, and slanderers. <div eID="gen17540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17541" type="x-p"/> (1.) That God's honour was interested in this case: <hi type="italic">Know,</hi> and make it known, <hi type="italic">that for thy sake I have suffered rebuke.</hi> Those that lay themselves open to reproach by their own fault and folly have great reason to bear it patiently, but no reason to expect that God should appear for them. But if it is for doing well that we suffer ill, and for righteousness' sake that we have all manner of evil said against us, we may hope that God will vindicate our honour with his own. To the same purport (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am called by thy name, O Lord of hosts!</hi> It was for that reason that his enemies hated him, and therefore for that reason he promised himself that God would own him and stand by him. <div eID="gen17541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17542" type="x-p"/> (2.) That the word of God, which he was employed to preach to others, he had experienced the power and pleasure of in his own soul, and therefore had the graces of the Spirit to qualify him for the divine favour, as well as his gifts. We find some rejected of God who yet could say, <hi type="italic">Lord, we have prophesied in thy name.</hi> But Jeremiah could say more (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thy words were found,</hi> found <hi type="italic">by me</hi>" (he searched the scripture, diligently studied the law, and found that in it which was reviving to him: if we seek we shall find), "found <hi type="italic">for me</hi>" (the words which he was to deliver to others were laid ready to his hand, were brought to him by inspiration), "<hi type="italic">and I did</hi> not only taste them, but <hi type="italic">eat them,</hi> received them entirely, conversed with them intimately; they were welcome to me, as food to one that is hungry; I entertained them, digested them, turned them <hi type="italic">in succum et sanguinem—into blood and spirits,</hi> and was myself delivered into the mould of those truths which I was to deliver to others." The prophet was told to <hi type="italic">eat the roll,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.8">Ezek. ii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.10.9">Rev. x. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">I did eat it</hi>—that is, as it follows, it <hi type="italic">was to me the joy and rejoicing of my heart,</hi> nothing could be more agreeable. Understand it, [1.] Of the message itself which he was to deliver. Though he was to foretel the ruin of his country, which was dear to him, and in the ruin of which he could not but have a deep share, yet all natural affections were swallowed up in zeal for God's glory, and even these messages of wrath, being divine messages, were a satisfaction to him. He also rejoiced, at first, in hope that the people would take warning and prevent the judgment. Or, [2.] Of the commission he received to deliver this message. Though the work he was called to was not attended with any secular advantages, but, on the contrary, exposed him to contempt and persecution, yet, because it put him in a way to serve God and do good, he took pleasure in it, was glad to be so employed, and it was his <hi type="italic">meat and drink to do the will of him that sent him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.34">John iv. 34</reference>. Or, [3.] Of the promise God gave him that he would assist and own him in his work (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.18">ch. i. 8</reference>); he was satisfied in that, and depended upon it, and therefore hoped it should not fail him. <div eID="gen17542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17543" type="x-p"/> (3.) That he had applied himself to the duty of his office with all possible gravity, seriousness, and self-denial, though he had had of late but little satisfaction in it, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.17">v. 17</reference>. [1.] It was his comfort that he had given up himself wholly to the business of his office and had done nothing either to divert himself from it or disfit himself for it. He kept no unsuitable company, denied himself the use even of lawful recreations, abstained from every thing that looked like levity, lest thereby he should make himself mean and less regarded. He <hi type="italic">sat alone,</hi> spent a great deal of time in his closet, <hi type="italic">because of the hand</hi> of the Lord that was strong upon him to carry him on his work, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.14">Ezek. iii. 14</reference>. "<hi type="italic">For thou hast filled me with indignation,</hi> with such messages of wrath against this people as have made me always pensive." Note, It will be a comfort to God's ministers, when men despise them, if they have the testimony of their consciences for them that they have not by any vain foolish behaviour made themselves despicable, that they have been dead not only to the wealth of the world, as this prophet was (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.10">v. 10</reference>), but to the pleasures of it too, as here. But, [2.] It is his complaint that he had had but little pleasure in his work. It was at first the rejoicing of his heart, but of late it had made him melancholy, so that he had no heart to <hi type="italic">sit in the meeting of those that make merry.</hi> He cared not for company, for indeed no company cared for him. He <hi type="italic">sat alone,</hi> fretting at the people's obstinacy and the little success of his labours among them. This filled him with a holy <hi type="italic">indignation.</hi> Note, It is the folly and infirmity of some good people that they lose much of the pleasantness of their religion by the fretfulness and uneasiness of their natural temper, which they humour and indulge, instead of mortifying it. <div eID="gen17543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17544" type="x-p"/> (4.) He throws himself upon God's pity and promise in a very passionate expostulation (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why is my pain perpetual,</hi> and nothing done to ease it? Why are the wounds which my enemies are continually giving both to my peace and to my reputation incurable, and nothing done to retrieve either my comfort or my credit? I once little thought that I should be thus neglected; will the God that has promised me his presence <hi type="italic">be to me as a liar,</hi> the God on whom I depend to be me <hi type="italic">as waters that fail?</hi>" We are willing to make the best we can of it, and to take it as an appeal, [1.] To the mercy of God: "I know he will not let the pain of his servant be perpetual, but he will ease it, will not let his wound be incurable, but he will heal it; and therefore I will not despair." [2.] To his faithfulness: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou be to me as a liar?</hi> No; I know thou wilt not. God is not a man that he should lie. The fountain of life will never be to his people as <hi type="italic">waters that fail.</hi>" <div eID="gen17544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17545" type="x-p"/> II. God's gracious answer to this address, <reference osisRef="Jer.15.19-Jer.15.21">v. 19-21</reference>. Though the prophet betrayed much human frailty in his address, yet God vouchsafed to answer him with good words and comfortable words; for he knows our frame. Observe, <div eID="gen17545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17546" type="x-p"/> 1. What God here requires of him as the condition of the further favours he designed him. Jeremiah had done and suffered much for God, yet God is no debtor to him, but he is still upon his good behaviour. God will own him. But, (1.) He must recover his temper, and be reconciled to his work, and friends with it again, and not quarrel with it any more as he had done. He must <hi type="italic">return,</hi> must shake off these distrustful discontented thoughts and passions, and not give way to them, must regain the peaceable possession and enjoyment of himself, and resolve to be easy. Note, When we have stepped aside into any disagreeable frame or way our care must be to return and compose ourselves into a right temper of mind again; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> we may expect God will help us, if thus we endeavour to help ourselves. (2.) He must resolve to be faithful in his work, for he could not expect the divine protection any longer than he did approve himself so. Though there was no cause at all to charge Jeremiah with unfaithfulness, and God knew his heart to be sincere, yet God saw fit to give him this caution. Those that do their duty must not take it ill to be told their duty. In two things he must be faithful:—[1.] He must distinguish between some and others of those he preached to: Thou must <hi type="italic">take forth the precious from the vile.</hi> The righteous are the precious be they ever so mean and poor; the wicked are the vile be they ever so rich and great. In our congregations these are mixed, wheat and chaff in the same floor; we cannot distinguish them by name, but we must by character, and must give to each a portion, speaking comfort to precious saints and terror to vile sinners, neither <hi type="italic">making the heart of the righteous sad</hi> nor <hi type="italic">strengthening the hands of the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.13.22">Ezek. xiii. 22</reference>), but <hi type="italic">rightly dividing the word of truth.</hi> Ministers must take those whom they see to be precious into their bosoms, and not <hi type="italic">sit alone</hi> as Jeremiah did, but keep up conversation with those they may do good to and get good by. [2.] He must closely adhere to his instructions, and not in the least vary from them: <hi type="italic">Let them return to thee, but return not thou to them,</hi> that is, he must do the utmost he can, in his preaching, to bring people up to the mind of God; he must tell them they must, at their peril, comply with that. Those that had flown off from him, that did not like the terms upon which God's favour was offered to them, "<hi type="italic">Let them return to thee,</hi> and, upon second thoughts, come up to the terms and strike the bargain; but do not thou <hi type="italic">return to them,</hi> do not compliment them, nor comply with them, nor think to make the matter easier to them than the word of God has made it." Men's hearts and lives must come up to God's law and comply with that, for God's law will never come down to them nor comply with them. <div eID="gen17546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17547" type="x-p"/> 2. What God here promises to him upon the performance of these conditions. If he approve himself well, (1.) God will tranquilize his mind and pacify the present tumult of his spirits: <hi type="italic">If thou return, I will bring thee again,</hi> will <hi type="italic">restore thy soul,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Ps. xxiii. 3</reference>. The best and strongest saints, if at any time they have gone aside out of the right way, and are determined to return, need the grace of God to bring them again. (2.) God will employ him in his service as a prophet, whose work, even in those bad times, had comfort and honour enough in it to be its own wages: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt stand before me,</hi> to receive instructions from me, as a servant from his master; and <hi type="italic">thou shalt be as my mouth</hi> to deliver my messages to the people, as an ambassador is the mouth of the prince that sends him." Note, Faithful ministers are God's mouth to us; they are so to look upon themselves, and to speak God's mind and <hi type="italic">as becomes the oracles of God;</hi> and we are so to look upon them, and to hear God speaking to us by them. Observe, If thou keep close to thy instructions, <hi type="italic">thou shalt be as my mouth,</hi> not otherwise; so far, and no further, God will stand by ministers, as they go by the written word. "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be as my mouth,</hi> that is, what thou sayest shall be made good, as if I myself had said it." See <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.19">1 Sam. iii. 19</reference>. (3.) He shall have strength and courage to face the many difficulties he meets with in his work, and his spirit shall not fail again as now it does (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will make thee unto this people as a fenced brazen wall,</hi> which the storm batters and beats violently upon, but cannot shake. <hi type="italic">Return not thou to them</hi> by any sinful compliances, and then trust thy God to arm thee by his grace with holy resolutions. Be not cowardly, and God will make thee daring." He had complained that he was made a <hi type="italic">man of strife.</hi> "Expect to be so (says God); they will <hi type="italic">fight against thee,</hi> they will still continue their opposition, <hi type="italic">but they shall not prevail against thee</hi> to drive thee off from thy work nor to cut thee off from the land of the living." (4.) He shall have God for his protector and mighty deliverer: <hi type="italic">I am with thee to save thee.</hi> Those that have God with them have a Saviour with them who has wisdom and strength enough to deal with the most formidable enemy; and those that are with God, and faithful to him, he will deliver (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.21">v. 21</reference>) either from trouble or through it. They may perhaps fall <hi type="italic">into the hand of the wicked,</hi> and they may appear terrible to them, but God will rescue them <hi type="italic">out of their hands.</hi> They shall not be able to kill them till they have finished their testimony; they shall not prevent their happiness. God will so deliver them as to <hi type="italic">preserve them to his heavenly kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 18</reference>), and that is deliverance enough. There are many things that appear very frightful that yet do not prove at all hurtful to a good man.  <chapter eID="Jer.15"/> <div eID="gen17547" type="x-p"/>

entries.c9d792ce3014895a1ccd02022f9a2fdc6939cf4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9928"/><div sID="gen17641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9928"/><hi type="bold">4. cause ... to be removed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.28.25">De 28:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.46">Eze 23:46</reference>). Rather, "I will give them up to vexation," I will cause them to wander so as nowhere to have repose [Calvin]; (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.8">2Ch 29:8</reference>, "trouble;" Margin, "commotion").<div eID="gen17641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of Manasseh--</hi>He was now dead, but the effects of his sins still remained. How much evil one bad man can cause! The evil fruits remain even after he himself has received repentance and forgiveness. The people had followed his wicked example ever since; and it is implied that it was only through the long-suffering of God that the penal consequences had been suspended up to the present time (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.16">1Ki 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.11">2Ki 21:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">23:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.3">24:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen17642" type="x-p"/>
